Main data and methods used for Roberts et al. (2026) - "Assessing upper bounds for solar-powered Controlled Environment Agriculture on existing cropland" Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems 10:1945186 Methods - CEA energy demand model setup To compare CEA powered by PV with crop-specific production globally, we derived a spatially-explicit energy demand per CEA. This type of comparison has been addressed in localized contexts in Weidner et al.[19], but lack a global scope as indicated in Bomford[23], Righini et al.[24,37], and Stanghellini & Katzin[27]. While there are many different greenhouse production models available[38], the specific aim of this study was to examine CEA systems and energy use on a global scale and this led to the construction of a model to address this aim. We developed a simple mechanistic model similar to the Van Henten model[39,40] as a way of incorporating experimental CEA crop production values and parameters[24] across a global spatial array (Supplementary Fig. 2). In order to make the model globally applicable, we made certain elements more generalized than they might be in a site-specific model, such as the building design, crop growing parameters and production system, building interaction with outside conditions, and the indoor environment control systems. The CEA yields, harvest metrics, and light requirements were taken directly from Righini et al.[24]. In that study, the authors compiled and analysed CEA metrics across multiple studies as well as their own experiments for wheat[28–30], soybean[24], potato[28,31,32], and tomato[24]. CEA aims to homogenize crop outputs and yields regardless of the geographic location, seasons, and local growing conditions. We applied this assumption to our model and kept CEA yields constant for each crop across the global spatial array. The yields from individual studies in Righini et al.[24] were analysed for parameters such as light requirements (photoperiod and photosynthetic photon flux density (PPFD)), the growing cycle length (days), and the resulting yields in terms of plant density, harvest index (ratio of harvested biomass to total plant biomass), fresh harvest yield per growing cycle, dry harvest yield per cycle, and annual fresh weight yield (as the sum of multiple growing cycles possible per year). The values from that study used in this CEA energy model are listed in Supplementary Table 2. Long-term and continuous datasets on CEA for different crops such as those included in this study were not available. Hence, we extrapolated from the experimental results that were available to assume multiple yields per year (3-4) that would be possible given the reported growing production times and days to harvest. The reference experimental studies all used soilless growing set-ups (e.g., hydroponic), so the same is assumed in our modelled CEA. Mills[34] also compared energy demands across CEA studies and found differences between and across crop types. Mills[34] acknowledges that for crops such as wheat, few studies are available and in some cases, there is a reliance on modelled crop simulations. Given the discrepancies and potentially large ranges between crops and individual studies, we chose to directly apply the RIghini et al. CEA data compilation as the main source of crop specific parameters. Two types of CEA were evaluated, a high-tech closed greenhouse (GH) and a vertical farm (VF), to model the energy required for each set-up to achieve the target yields as compiled in Righini et al.[24]. The mechanistic greenhouse model assumed uniform internal conditions, also known as a “perfectly stirred tank”[39], and considered water vapour and energy balances in a similar way to the Van Henten model[38–40] (Supplementary Tables 1 & 3). We adapted the basic greenhouse balance equations for energy and water vapour from the van Henten model[39,40] to run the simplified model on global scales to calculate the CEA energy demand: dE/dt = QSun + QHeat + QLamp - QVent - QLatent - QCon – QFIR – Qcool (J m-2 s-1 = W m-2) dMW/dt = WTrans + WEvap + WHum - WCond - WVent - WDehum (kg {water vapor} m-2 s-1) dE/dt = net change of energy Q = rate of heat transfer from the various factors, inside and outside the growing space dMW/dt = net change of water mass W = rate of water vapor change over time from inside and outside factors More detailed processes can be captured in van Henten[39,40] or other greenhouse models[38]; however, to represent the major drivers of energy use, we only focused on these specific aspects. The process for calculating the influence of solar radiation was the same for both GH and VF and was an adapted version of the equation[24]: Energy Uselights = PPFD * photoperiod * 3600 * ηlights *10-6 (MJ m-2 day-1) ηlights= electrical efficacy The walls in the VF had 0% light entering, whereas the GH had 82% of solar radiation entering the growing space[22]. For incoming solar radiation, the daily total values were per month for an average daily solar radiation (J m-2 day-1). This incoming average daily solar radiation load was converted to a PPFD (μmol m-2 s-1) as the total daily PPFD or Daily Light Interval (DLI) as mol m-2 day-1. The PPFD and photoperiod for each crop from Righini et al.[24] was converted into a DLI requirement per day. The difference between the actual DLI and this required DLI indicated the lighting (J m-2 day-1) shortfall. Dividing this shortfall by the electrical efficacy*16 of the lights gave the average daily supplemental lighting demand (MJ m-2 day-1) for each month of 2020. While there are other potential processes or factors that would contribute to CEA energy demand, such as water pumps and irrigation, mechanized automation, and computer and sensor controls, these are relatively minor compared to the major energy drivers such as supplemental lighting, growing space heating and cooling, and ventilation[24]. Between the two CEA set-ups, there were minor adjustments to the building dimensions, crop growing area, and wall insulation properties. The simplified building designs similar to Weidner et al.[19,41] were intended to capture the basic parameters of the indoor growing space and basic interactions with the outdoor environment. In this way, the major drivers of CEA energy demand could be compared while avoiding specific building designs that vary by specific location and use. In this simulation, the vertical farm and closed greenhouse each had supplemental lighting, temperature, and humidity controls to maintain the same light requirements, indoor conditions, and annual yields depending on the crop requirements. The model considered a 1 ha GH (75% of the building footprint is considered usable as growing area) and a 0.25 ha VF (with 4 stacked layers that utilize 75% of the building footprint for growing area). The VF yield was assumed to be four times per hectare of building footprint compared to the GH as a way to capture the increased production capacity potential for the VF. Additionally, the VF was assumed to be 8m in height and the GH was assumed to be 4m in height. The same indoor environment was assumed for both systems and in turn the capacity to maintain that growing space environment is what drives the energy demand (Supplementary Table 1 & 3). We used the average daily light (PPFD) requirements, photoperiod, and annual yields according to Righini et al.[24] and included updated lighting and indoor environmental parameters to meet the best available standards for LEDs and heat pumps (Supplementary Table 4). The values presented by Righini et al.[24] include their own data for tomato and soybean experiments as well as a compilation of previous experiments for wheat[28–30] and potato[28,31,32] trials. Each of the selected experiments may have differed in specific CEA designs; however, all were soilless systems that relied entirely on supplemental lighting for crop growth. The mechanistic greenhouse model had a time-step of one day for all indoor processes. The outdoor climate conditions were averaged for each month and recorded as the average daily temperature, relative humidity, and solar radiation flux for each grid cell per month. The model received the daily average (for each month) as input data and first calculated the influence of the outside factors on the indoor growing parameters (temperature, relative humidity, and light) for both VF and GH. Then for each growing space parameter, the corresponding CEA component was forced to correct the factor to bring it back into the target range. For heating and cooling this was done with a heat pump, for relative humidity with humidifier or ventilation, and LEDs for supplemental lighting. The energy requirement for each component to maintain the target growing conditions was summed for each average day per month. These daily energy totals were multiplied by the number of days per month to return a monthly energy demand based on the average day in that month. These monthly values were then summed to return an annual energy demand. This annual energy demand was divided by the annual CEA yield per building to give the energy use efficiency (MJ kg-1) for each crop and CEA system. The resulting energy demand reflects the energy needed to maintain those constant internal conditions within the target ranges. By doing this, we were able to compare the plant specific growing parameters and yields from Righini et al.[24] between VF and GH systems. CEA energy demand simulation inputs The selected crops for the study were wheat, potato, soybean, and tomato to represent grain, legume, tuber, and vegetable crop types. The temperature control (15-23°C) and relative humidity range (60-85%) were set at levels similar to Weidner et al.[19,41] (Supplementary Table 3) We assumed a fixed biomass production per growing cycle and year (yield biomass per m2 and harvest index adapted from Righini et al.[24] instead of simulating crop growth over time and across growth stages. Because evapotranspiration is a complex process that varies between crops and plant stages, we applied a single generalised evapotranspiration rate of 4.5 mm day-1 for all crops[42–44]. Additionally, the energy to power water pumps and recirculation is relatively insignificant compared to other CEA processes and the water use itself might be over 90% lower (for both closed greenhouses and vertical farms) than comparable field systems[20,24,45]. For this reason, water use and energy for the irrigation and water pump and recirculation system were not included. A heat pump is used to maintain the internal temperature within the target range with a Coefficient of Performance, for heating, (COP) of 4.0 and an Energy Efficiency Ratio, for cooling, (EER) of 13.0[46]. These COP and EER are general values in order to reflect that these efficiencies could be influenced by local conditions and product designs. The building wall insulation R-value was kept at 3 for the GH[47] and 15 for the VF[48]. Supplemental lighting from LEDs was set to 3.5 mmol J-1 to represent the current best available standard[22,27] (Supplementary Table 4). ERA 5 Agrometeorological environmental data[49] (0.1° x 0.1° resolution) were used for daily measurements for solar radiation flux (J m-2), temperature (K at 2m height), and relative humidity (% at 2m height at 12h) for the year 2020. The daily values for each grid cell were averaged for each month in the year 2020. This averaged daily value per month for the climate parameters (solar radiation, temperature, relative humidity) were input into the CEA energy demand model at 1-day time steps. The use of a monthly averaged value for each climate factor was a trade-off to run the model efficiently on a global array while still capturing site and seasonal variations. The model outputs were calculated in total energy demand (MJ) per day and then summed for a monthly and annual total. The annual energy demand to crop yield (MJ kg-1) or energy use efficiency in each CEA system was then calculated per grid cell. Both monthly energy demand and annual energy use efficiency were downscaled to a 1km grid in order to compare to the higher resolution land use and solar PV potential model outputs. The resulting energy use efficiency as MJ kg-1 for each crop calculated by region for both CEA systems is shown in Fig. 2. Global crop area, yield, and production We used a data harmonisation approach based on the HILDA+ land use reconstruction model[2], to allocate 2020 crop production (t km-2) and crop harvest area (ha km-2) for the target crops to a 1km global grid array. This approach allowed us to harmonise the outputs of multiple crop models, datasets, and statistical inventories to produce crop area, yield, and production maps for each target crop. In HILDA+, the cropland areas were isolated and used to mask the CROPGRIDS crop-specific crop area data (reference year 2020)[36]. GAEZ v4 (reference year 2015)[35], along with the statistical data for FAO country level harvest area and production quantity totals (reference year 2020)[50] were used to assign the pixel-level harvest area (ha) and yields (t/ha) for the target crops. This was done by first normalizing the GAEZ v4 crop yield values, i.e. dividing them by their national and cropland-wide mean, as well as normalizing the CROPGRIDS crop area values by their national and cropland-wide sum (all constrained by HILDA+ cropland and at least 5% CROPGRIDS crop coverage). This normalization was done in order to align each input dataset with the same consistent spatial array and projection. The normalized values, crop yield and area, were then multiplied by FAO crop yield and harvested area in 2020, respectively. The crop production (t) was finally derived by a pixel-based multiplication of country- and crop-specific yield (t ha-1) and harvested areas (ha). Each crop then had a specific harvest area (ha), yield (t ha-1), and production (t) per grid cell for the year 2020. In order to harmonise these different datasets, steps were taken to minimise inter-dataset variability. FAO statistics only report crop area harvested, which could include multiple harvests on the same area, so the CROPGRIDS crop cultivation area layer was used to set a fraction of crop area per grid cell prior to allocating the FAO area harvested within each country’s grid cells. Upper thresholds for crop area were set to limit any instance where the area from multiple harvests were applied to the same grid cell. In this way we were able to remove inconsistencies or data artifacts that would otherwise inflate the crop area beyond what was available in the grid cell (i.e., more than 100 ha crop area for a 100 ha grid cell). The data harmonisation process of crop area, yield, and production is simplified in Supplementary Fig. 4. PV-powered CEA comparison with 2020 crop area, yield, and production The CEA crop yields[24] were kept constant across the global array in order to test the area and PV energy capacity to scale these experimental values globally. The multiple datasets[35,36,50] used across the analysis reported the reference yields and production in harvested biomass. For this reason, we used CEA production and yield values for harvested biomass. For different research questions, this metric could be changed to dry harvest weight, calories, or other specific nutritional or agronomic units. The first step to calculate the comparison against 2020 crop production was to determine the CEA building area needed to meet 2020 production (t km-2) per grid cell. The annual CEA yields were calculated per growing area and were set per grid cell to reflect the CEA systems (0.75ha growing area per 1ha GH building area and 0.75ha growing area per 0.25ha VF building area). The 2020 production array was divided by the annual CEA yield (per growing area) per crop to give the CEA building area needed for year-round CEA production in each grid cell. This CEA footprint requirement was summed per hectare for GH or per 0.25 hectare for VF per grid cell. To calculate the solar PV area needed for the CEA, the monthly solar PV potential (kWh m-2) was derived from Saxena et al.[33]. The area available for PV per grid cell was calculated as the harvest area subtracted by the CEA building area per grid cell. The surface area coverage of the solar PV was assumed to be 75% of a given area[22], so the potential energy available to the CEA was reduced by this factor. This PV potential was then multiplied by an efficiency factor[51] (26.8%) for conversion to usable electricity. The total CEA energy demand per building (1ha for GH and 0.25ha for VF) per grid cell was multiplied by the CEA building area requirement to calculate the total CEA energy demand per grid cell. The monthly PV area requirement to directly power the CEA was calculated by multiplying the potential PV energy by the CEA energy demand per grid cell. The process is summarized visually in Supplementary Fig. 3 and all CEA component inputs are summarized in Supplementary Tables 1-4. For year-round production, the month with the greatest PV area requirement for each grid cell became the fixed PV area needed to power the required CEA area for that grid cell. No energy storage was assumed from one day to the next, so each day had only the monthly 1-day average to fulfil the CEA demand. We also analysed continuous 9-month CEA production capacity as a way to reduce the energy demand and the required PV area to power the CEA. The reduction in yield capacity was taken into account and the CEA area needed to meet 2020-Production per grid cell was re-calculated. For the shortened 9-month production cycle, the 9-month stretch with the lowest PV area requirements to meet indoor energy demands were calculated per grid cell. Similar to the year-round production, the month with the greatest PV area requirement for this 9-month cycle, determined the PV area needed for that grid cell. The resulting area (ha) of PV needed to power a year-round or 9-month CEA is displayed spatially in Supplementary Fig. 7. This CEA building area plus PV area was the total area that was then compared to the crop harvest area per grid cell. The land area requirement balance (ha) was calculated by subtracting the CEA building footprint plus PV area from the crop area per grid cell. If the area balance was negative, then not enough area was available for the CEA-PV to meet 2020 production in that grid cell. If the balance was zero or positive, the CEA-PV matched 2020 production and any positive value could be considered a lower required land area than 2020 production area in ha. Only the grid cells with a positive area balance were used to calculate the potential extra or surplus production by allowing the model to utilise all crop area available and CEA production above 2020 production values. This extra-production was calculated by incrementally adding CEA units (1ha for GH and 0.25ha for VF) and the required PV area per building. This process was done iteratively until the crop harvest area in that grid cell reached zero. The sum of this extra production according to the CEA building area added, was then added to that grid cell total production quantity. The spatial distribution of areas where CEA met 2020 production can be seen in Fig. 3. The global totals and comparison between CEA systems for harvest area (ha) where CEA met 2020 production, production quantity (t) met by CEA, lower CEA-PV land area requirements compared to 2020 production (ha), and extra production (t) by CEA are given in Fig. 4. The regional breakdowns relative to the global totals as well as the breakdown within each region are given in Supplementary Figs. 8&9. Yield gap analysis The yield gap analysis and comparison were done to apply a single metric for comparing crop production challenges globally. For this study we used the GAEZ v4 crop-wise Yield Achievement Ratio[35] (YAR) global gridded (5 arc minutes) dataset for the most recent average (2009-2011). The YAR was calculated by GAEZ as the ratio of actual (average) yields to the attainable yields for each grid cell. The attainable yields were calculated as the biophysical influences (e.g., solar radiation, water, nutrients, temperature) on yield (potential yield) while considering location specific constraints (e.g., soil or terrain, pest pressure, management). For the crops analysed in this study, GAEZ only has YAR data for wheat, soybean, and potato, so we limited the yield gap analysis to these crops. The ratio of actual/ attainable yields is inversely proportional to the yield gap, as a higher ratio indicates a smaller yield gap. We used the GAEZ YAR data that had already been divided into bins corresponding to the crop-wise YAR. The 2020 crop-wise harvest area (ha) was compared to the corresponding YAR to calculate the distribution of crop harvest area per YAR bin. This distribution (percent of harvest area (ha)) per YAR bin was plotted to complement the global YAR maps plotted directly from the GAEZ dataset. CEA-PV system performance compared to 2020 production was then evaluated against the reference crop yield gaps. Only grid cells where there was spatial agreement between the CROPGRIDS and GAEZ YAR datasets were considered. To analyse CEA-PV relationships with crop yield gaps, only the grid cells where CEA-PV demonstrated the ability to meet 2020 production were considered. Including only these CEA-PV net area positive areas was done to focus on the technical potential of CEA in alleviating yield gap constraints. In our analysis, CEA-PV net negative could not meet the same production values as 2020 production without additional crop area, it was assumed that CEA in these areas would be able to aid in yield gap closures. The area (ha) that was net positive CEA-PV crop area was summed for each YAR bin and the percent of the net positive CEA-PV crop area was plotted alongside the total crop harvest area distribution. Supplementary Fig. 1 provides a general overview of the yield gap analysis process. Electricity grid constraints The Arderne et al.[52] electrical grid dataset was used to evaluate the current electrical grid coverage in areas that overlap with areas that meet 2020 production (CEA-PV technical capacity areas). Where there was at least medium-voltage electricity, a 2km buffer was set as the maximum distance for connection to these electricity grids. The grid cells where there was overlap of this grid network and buffer with these CEA-PV grid cells that met 2020 production were summed, as well as those that were outside of this 2km buffer. The grid cells were then multiplied by the crop harvest area (ha) in that grid cell and then summed crop at the country- and regional-levels. The proportion of harvest area (ha) where CEA met 2020 production within the 2km electricity grid was then calculated for country and region as seen in Fig. 5. The spatial overlap of areas where CEA met 2020 production and the electricity grid can be seen in Supplementary Fig. 10. Aridity Index The Global Aridity Index Database as described in Zomer et al.(52) was used to compare where CEA matched 2020 production against aridity zones. The aridity index was divided into bins according to the index value. These index values were overlaid on the grid cells where CEA matched 2020 production. The harvest area (ha) was then multiplied by the number of grid cells within each index bin. The harvest area (ha) where CEA matched 2020 production was plotted according to the aridity index bin and results are given in Supplementary Fig. 11. Model assumption sensitivity A deterministic sensitivity analysis was conducted to evaluate CEA-PV equivalent capacity reactions to changes in model assumptions. The sensitivity analysis evaluated changing assumptions around three parameters directly influencing CEA-PV area requirements and subsequent equivalent-capacity calculations: CEA crop yield, CEA energy demand, and PV conversion efficiency. Changes to each assumption were considered individually and for their combined effects on CEA-PV equivalent capacity. The main “baseline” analysis for GH and VF applied the experimental CEA yields described above and calculated the CEA building area required to match 2020 crop production in each grid cell, while the PV area requirement was determined from the corresponding CEA energy demand and a baseline PV conversion efficiency of 26.8%. For the yield sensitivity analysis, the annual CEA yield for each crop was reduced by 10%, 25%, and 50%. The required CEA building area was then recalculated directly from 2020 crop production using the reduced yield while retaining the same GH- or VF-specific growing areas and corresponding year-round or 9-month growing cycles. The greater CEA area required under lower yields also increased growing area and associated PV area requirements to match 2020 crop production. For the energy sensitivity, CEA energy demand per unit growing area was increased by 10%, 25%, and 50%, while CEA yields and building area requirements were maintained at baseline input values. In turn, the corresponding PV area requirement increased to meet the increased energy demand. For the PV efficiency sensitivity, conversion efficiency was reduced from the baseline input value of 26.8% to 22%, while CEA crop yields and energy demands were kept constant. The PV area requirements were then required to provide the same amount of energy to meet CEA energy demands. Additionally, the joint effects of combining CEA yield reductions, energy demand increases, and PV conversion efficiency reductions were evaluated. For each joint effect scenario, the revised CEA building area and PV requirements were compared to the available crop-wise harvested area in each grid cell using the same approach as the baseline analysis to calculate equivalent capacity. The sensitivity analysis tested the change in absolute area (ha), production (t), and less crop area required (ha) and corresponding global percentages for the CEA systems, year-round and 9-month growing cycles, and four crops. The sensitivity analysis therefore tested how these CEA systems performed under less favourable model assumptions rather than representing probabilistic uncertainty ranges. The ASILaC datasets presents monthly files of correlation statistics calculated between Sea Ice Area (SIA) in eight Arctic basins and terrestrial parameters in the Arctic region North of 60°N. Data format: raster GeoTIFF The terrestrial parameters are: 1. Permafrost Ground Temperature at 2m depth 2000-2019 (source: Obu et al. (2023)) 2. Maximum NDVI (MaxNDVI) based on MODIS 2000-2019 (Source: Tommervik (2025)) 3. Time Integrated NDVI (TINDVI) based on MODIS 2000-2019 (Source: Tommervik (2025)) 4. Snow Water Equivalent (SWE) 2000-2018 based on SSMI (Source: Luojus et al. (2021)) Sea ice area data for 2000-2019 have been obtained from OSI SAF (OSI SAF 2020). De-trending has been applied to all parameters. The correlation (r) has been filtered at significance level p_value < 0.05. Each file referring to subbasins contains 6 bands: Band 1: minimum correlation value Band 2: maximum correlation value Band 3: associated basin with minimum correlation value Band 4: associated basin with maximum correlation value Band 5: mean correlation value Band 6: standard deviation Each file referring to the entire NH sea ice area contains 1 band: Band 1: correlation value Bartsch, A., Tanguy, R., Bergstedt, H., von Baeckmann, C., Tømmervik, H., Macias-Fauria, M., Lemmetyinen, J., Rautiainen, K., Gruber, C., and Forbes, B. The Arctic land parameter trend datasets cover the Arctic region North of 60°N. Consistent masking for ice sheets and water bodies has been applied. Datasets are organized by source/parameter. When evaluating the seismic hazard within a region or site of interest (e.g., a densely populated city or a nuclear power plant), it is essential to realistically model the characteristics (size, geometry and surface orientation) of large earthquake ruptures that may occur. The GEESE algorithm retrieves sufficiently representative ruptures for queried earthquakes from seismic hazard models developed within the OpenQuake Engine seismic hazard software. We used the GEESE algorithm to retrieve finite ruptures for the strongest events included in the global-coverage ISC-GEM earthquake catalogue (covering a time window of 1904 to 2019), which we present here as the GEESE database. For each event to which a rupture could be retrieved, the database also included the inputs for an OpenQuake Hazard Scenario calculation and the ground-motion fields (GMFs) computed using some (reconfigurable) default parameters. The GEESE algorithm and database is described in detail in the following open-access journal article: Brooks, C., Pagani, M., Villani, M., Johnson, K., Styron, R., & Bayliss, K. (2025). Global EarthquakE ScEnarios (GEESE): An OpenQuake Engine-Based Rupture Matching Algorithm and Scenarios Database for Seismic Source Model Testing and Rapid Post-Event Response Analysis. Seismica, 4(2). https://doi.org/10.26443/seismica.v4i2.1654

Overview This dataset contains version 3.0 (March 2025 release) of the Global Fishing Watch apparent fishing effort dataset. Data is available for 2012-2024 and based on positions of >190,000 unique automatic identification system (AIS) devices on fishing vessels, of which up to ~96,000 are active in a given year. Fishing vessels are identified via a machine learning model, vessel registry databases, and manual review by GFW and regional experts. Vessel time is measured in hours, calculated by assigning to each AIS position the amount of time elapsed since the previous AIS position of the vessel. The time is counted as apparent fishing hours if the GFW fishing detection model - a neural network machine learning model - determines the vessel is engaged in fishing behavior during that AIS position. Data are spatially binned into grid cells that measure 0.01 or 0.1 degrees on a side; the coordinates defining each cell are provided in decimal degrees (WGS84) and correspond to the lower-left corner. Data are available in the following formats: Daily apparent fishing hours by flag state and gear type at 100th degree resolution Monthly apparent fishing hours by flag state and gear type at 10th degree resolution Daily apparent fishing hours by MMSI at 10th degree resolution The fishing effort dataset is accompanied by a table of vessel information (e.g. gear type, flag state, dimensions). File structure Fishing effort and vessel presence data are available as .csv files in daily formats. Files for each year are stored in separate .zip files. A README.txt and schema.json file is provided for each dataset version and contains the table schema and additional information. There is also a README-known-issues-v3.txt file outlining some of the known issues with the version 3 release. Files are names according to the following convention: Daily file format: [fleet/mmsi]-daily-csvs-[100/10]-v3-[year].zip [fleet/mmsi]-daily-csvs-[100/10]-v3-[date].csv Monthly file format: fleet-monthly-csvs-10-v3-[year].zip fleet-monthly-csvs-10-v3-[date].csv Fishing vessel format: fishing-vessels-v3.csv README file format: README-[fleet/mmsi/fishing-vessels/known-issues]-v3.txt File identifiers: [fleet/mmsi]: Data by fleet (flag and geartype) or by MMSI [100/10]: 100th or 10th degree resolution [year]: Year of data included in .zip file [date]: Date of data included in .csv files. For monthly data, [date]corresponds to the first date of the month Examples: fleet-daily-csvs-100-v3-2020.zip; mmsi-daily-csvs-10-v3-2020-01-10.csv; fishing-vessels-v3.csv; README-fleet-v3.txt; fleet-monthly-csvs-10-v3-2024.zip; fleet-monthly-csvs-10-v3-2024-08-01.csv Key documentation For an overview of how GFW turns raw AIS positions into estimates of fishing hours, see this page. The models used to produce this dataset were developed as part of this publication: D.A. Kroodsma, J. Mayorga, T. Hochberg, N.A. Miller, K. Boerder, F. Ferretti, A. Wilson, B. Bergman, T.D. White, B.A. Block, P. Woods, B. Sullivan, C. Costello, and B. Worm. "Tracking the global footprint of fisheries." Science 361.6378 (2018). Model details are available in the Supplementary Materials. The README-known-issues-v3.txt file describing this dataset's specific caveats can be downloaded from this page. We highly recommend that users read this file in full. The README-mmsi-v3.txt file, the README-fleet-v3.txt file, and the README-fishing-vessels-v3.txt files are downloadable from this page and contain the data description for (respectively) the fishing hours by MMSI dataset, the fishing hours by fleet dataset, and the vessel information file. These readmes contain key explanations about the gear types and flag states assigned to vessels in the dataset. File name structure for the datafiles are available below on this page and file schema can be downloaded from this page. A FAQ describing the updates in this version and the differences between this dataset and the data available from the GFW Map and APIs is available here. Use Cases The apparent fishing hours dataset is intended to allow users to analyze patterns of fishing across the world’s oceans at temporal scales as fine as daily and at spatial scales as fine as 0.1 or 0.01 degree cells. Fishing hours can be separated out by gear type, vessel flag and other characteristics of vessels such as tonnage. Potential applications for this dataset are broad. We offer suggested use cases to illustrate its utility. The dataset can be integrated as a static layer in multi-layered analyses, allowing researchers to investigate relationships between fishing effort and other variables, including biodiversity, tracking, and environmental data, as defined by their research objectives. A few example questions that these data could be used to answer: What flag states have fishing activity in my area of interest? Do hotspots of longline fishing overlap with known migration routes of sea turtles? How does fishing time by trawlers change by month in my area of interest? Which seasons see the most trawling hours and which see the least? Caveats This global dataset estimates apparent fishing hours effort. The dataset is based on publicly available information and statistical classifications which may not fully capture the nuances of local fishing practices. While we manually review the dataset at a global scale and in a select set of smaller test regions to check for issues, given the scale of the dataset we are unable to manually review every fleet in every region. We recognize the potential for inaccuracies and encourage users to approach regional analyses with caution, utilizing their own regional expertise to validate findings. We welcome your feedback on any regional analysis at research@globalfishingwatch.org to enhance the dataset's accuracy. Caveats relating to known sources of inaccuracy as well as interpretation pitfalls to avoid are described in the README-known-issues-v3.txt file available for download from this page. We highly recommend that users read this file in full. The issues described include: Data from 2024 should be considered provisional, as vessel classifications may change as more data from 2025 becomes available. MMSI is used in this dataset as the vessel identifier. While MMSI is intended to serve as the unique AIS identifier for an individual vessel, this does not always hold in practice. The Maritime Identification Digits (MID), the first 3 digits of MMSI, are the only source of information on vessel flag state when the vessel does not appear on a registry. The MID may be entered incorrectly, obscuring information about an MMSI’s flag state. AIS reception is not consistent across all areas and changes over time. Alternative ways to access Query using SQL in the Global Fishing Watch public BigQuery dataset: global-fishing-watch.fishing_effort_v3 Download the entire dataset from the Global Fishing Watch Data Download Portal (https://globalfishingwatch.org/data-download/datasets/public-fishing-effort)

Description The products are experimental datasets of long-term (approximately 20 years) Irrigation Water Use at 0.25° resolution. They cover four regions: the Contiguous United States (CONUS), the Ebro River Basin in north-eastern Spain, the Murray-Darling Basin in south-eastern Australia, and India. These datasets are the outcome of the European Space Agency (ESA) Climate Change Initiative Anthropogenic Water Use (CCI-AWU) precursor project (project link). They were produced using three different methods: SM-based (Soil-Moisture-based) Inversion, SM-based Delta, and Model-Observation Integration, which is based on the Noah-Multiparameterization model. The SM-based Inversion method was used to produce five datasets for the four regions, each using a different SM product as input. These include ESA CCI Combined, ESA CCI Passive, ASCAT (Advanced Scatterometer), SMOS (Soil Moisture and Ocean Salinity), and SMAP (Soil Moisture Active Passive). The SM-based Delta method was used to produce six datasets for the four regions, each combining different SM and evapotranspiration (ET) products as input. The combinations include ESA CCI Combined SM & FLUXCOM ET, ESA CCI Passive SM & FLUXCOM ET, ESA CCI Active SM & FLUXCOM ET, ESA CCI Combined SM & SSEBOP ET, ESA CCI Passive SM & SSEBOP ET, and ESA CCI Active SM & SSEBOP ET. The Model-Observation Integration method was applied to the CONUS and Murray-Darling Basin regions, producing three datasets using different irrigated surface maps as input. These maps include the Landsat-Derived Global Rainfed and Irrigated-Cropland Product (referred to as "Landsat", the Relative Bias Approach (referred to as "Method1"), and the Multi-Resolution Analysis Approach (referred to as "Method2"). The irrigation products are delivered with monthly temporal aggregation. Acknowledgements: The datasets were developed as part of the ESA CCI-AWU precursor project (contract no. 4000142449/23/I-NB).
keywords: Irrigation; Remote sensing; Satellite; Model; SM-based; Irrigation water; Soil moisture; Evapotranspiration

Description COPOSIS is an aggregation of four soil texture dataset covering North America at a 0.1 degree resolution. COPOSIS stems from CONABIO, POLARIS, SIIGSOL and SoilGrids, the four components of the dataset. COPOSIS contains Sand and Clay content of soils (in %) for 6 soil depth intervals. The depth intervals are 0-5cm, 5-15cm, 15-30cm, 30-60cm, 60-100cm, 100-200cm. The border of each component of the COPOSIS is filtered to remove apparent geopolitical borders from the data set. The Global Reservoir Sedimentation Rate (GRSR) dataset, developed using the Integrated Reservoir Sedimentation Prediction (IRSP) model, integrates data from Global Dam Watch (GDW) version 1.0, the Original Reservoir Sedimentation Survey Information System (RESIS), academic publications, and water resource agency reports. It provides reservoir sedimentation rate (RSR) estimates for 34,372 reservoirs worldwide, with a total storage capacity of 7,284 km³. This dataset is associated with the study by Gong et al., "Quantifying Global Reservoir Sedimentation Rates," Geophysical Research Letters (under review, 2025).
keywords: Remote Sensing; Hydrology; Water Resources Management

description: Open-access database of englacial temperature measurements compiled from data submissions and published literature. It is developed on GitHub and published to Zenodo. This version (1.0.0) of the dataset is described in the following publication: Mylène Jacquemart, Ethan Welty, Marcus Gastaldello, and Guillem Carcanade (2025). glenglat: A database of global englacial temperatures. Earth System Science Data 17(4): 1627–1666. https://doi.org/10.5194/essd-17-1627-2025 Dataset structure The dataset adheres to the Frictionless Data Tabular Data Package specification. The metadata in datapackage.json describes, in detail, the contents of the tabular data files in the data folder: source.csv: Description of each data source (either a personal communication or the reference to a published study). borehole.csv: Description of each borehole (location, elevation, etc), linked to source.csv via source_id and less formally via source identifiers in notes. profile.csv: Description of each profile (date, etc), linked to borehole.csv via borehole_id and to source.csv via source_id and less formally via source identifiers in notes. measurement.csv: Description of each measurement (depth and temperature), linked to profile.csv via borehole_id and profile_id. For boreholes with many profiles (e.g. from automated loggers), pairs of profile.csv and measurement.csv are stored separately in subfolders of data named {source.id}-{glacier}, where glacier is a simplified and kebab-cased version of the glacier name (e.g. flowers2022-little-kluane). Supporting information The folder sources, available on GitHub but omitted from dataset releases on Zenodo, contains subfolders (with names matching column source.id) with files that document how and from where the data was extracted. Tables Jump to: source · borehole · profile · measurement source Sources of information considered in the compilation of this database. Zagorodnov]) and non-English titles are followed by a translation in square brackets. description: PATRIS (Parameterization of Trentino forest types by rapid forest inventory) The dataset consists of relascopic measurements (807 plots) and forest structure parameters (LAI, clumping index, gap fraction by zenith angle range) derived from hemispheric photos over 401 plots in the province of Trento. A severe windstorm in October 2018 (Vaia storm) caused extensive windthrows over 20 thousand hectares in most forest areas of the province, including those included in the dataset. description: Readme file content: These data are simulation results generated using the ORCHIDEE-CNP model (version: SVN r7744) for the ICONICA project sites (https://forge.ipsl.jussieu.fr/orchidee/wiki/GroupActivities/CodeAvalaibilityPublication/ORCHIDEE_CN-P-MIMICS_7301). The dataset includes simulations for three European grassland research sites located in Ireland, the Netherlands, and Sweden. Detailed information about the Irish site can be found in Sheil et al. (2016) and Tunney et al. (2009), while the Swedish site is described in Simonsson et al. (2018). Information on the Netherlands site is available in Van Der Salm et al. (2009, 2017) and Van Middelkoop et al. (2016). For each site, simulations were conducted under four phosphorus (P) addition levels: No P addition (no P addition) Low P addition (2.5 g m⁻² yr⁻¹) Medium P addition (5.0 g m⁻² yr⁻¹) High P addition (10.0 g m⁻² yr⁻¹) Simulated variables include: Year average Yield: Yield (g C/m²/day) Year average SOC: Soil Organic Carbon (g C/m²) Year average CO₂: Soil CO₂ Emission (g C/m²/day) Year average SOP: Soil Organic P (g/m²) Year average LAP: Soil Labile P (g/m²) Daily average N₂O emissions: N₂O Emission (g N₂O-N/m²/day) The data set covers the period 1968 to 2020, with the exception of daily N₂O emissions, which covers the period 2016 to 2020. Simulation Setup: The simulation setup accounts for the effect of changing climate and increasing atmospheric carbon dioxide concentration on the biogeochemical cycles since 1900 assuming constant present day land use. Atmospheric nitrogen and phosphorus addition was set to reconstructions for the year 1990 and kept constant throughout the simulations. The forcing data was used from the 10th installment of the Trendy model intercomparison for the Global Carbon Budget update for 2019 (Friedlingstein et al. 2020). Site-level meteorological data (6 hourly temperature, precipitation, radiation, humidity, and wind speed) and atmospheric nutrient deposition were used as forcing inputs and extracted from global reconstruction based on the site locations. Spin-up phase: A spin-up simulation (3000 years) was conducted using recycled climate data until carbon and nutrient pools reached a steady state. Transient phase: Historical transient simulations were performed from 1901 to 2020 using site-specific reconstructed climate and atmospheric carbon dioxide concentration. Phosphorus treatments: Dedicated simulation restarting from the transient phase simulation of the year of the onset of phosphorus trials were conducted for each of the phosphorus treatments at each site by prescribing constant phosphorus inputs. Model Version: Simulations were conducted using the ORCHIDEE-CNP model, version SVN r7744 (Goll et al 2021). Acknowledgements: This dataset was produced as part of the ICONICA project. We acknowledge the support from partner institutions and collaborators at the ICONICA experimental sites. References: Friedlingstein, P., et al., 2020. Global Carbon Budget 2020. Earth Syst. Sci. description: Vegetation spring phenology signals the start of vegetation functional recovery in ecosystems and plays a vital role in shaping the global carbon cycle. Among key spring phenological events, leaf growth directly influences carbon dioxide exchange on a global scale. However, the extent to which photosynthetic carbon assimilation in one year influences leaf growth in the subsequent year remains difficult to quantify. Using satellite-derived leaf area index (LAI) data, we estimated the start of the growing season (SOS) and the peak of the growing season (POS), dividing the leaf growth process into two components: leaf area increment (∆LAI) and leaf growth duration (∆DOY). Our results show that ∆LAI in northern ecosystems is experiencing a significant upward trend, with over 10.7% of the region exhibiting ∆LAI growth rates exceeding 0.2 m2 m–2 year–1. This trend is primarily driven by solar radiation and photosynthetic carbon assimilation. In contrast, ∆DOY shows only a slight shortening trend, with most changes ranging from –0.2 to 0.2 days year–1. Moreover, the influence of photosynthetic carbon assimilation on ∆DOY appears minimal, likely because photosynthesis affects the timing of both SOS and POS simultaneously. Our findings demonstrate that photosynthetic carbon assimilation primarily drives leaf area expansion, with limited effects on leaf growth duration in northern ecosystems. This study contributes to advancing vegetation phenology theories, emphasizing that accurately quantifying the impacts of photosynthetic carbon assimilation is crucial for improving future predictions of vegetation seasonality and the carbon cycle.

Motivated by the need to improve the representation of small-scale surface heterogeneity in Earth System Models (ESMs), new algorithms have been introduced to discretize ESM computational units into a variable number of subgrid topographic units for improving model simulations with minimal increase in computational demand. The algorithms can be applied to both structured (regular grid) and unstructured (e.g., watersheds) computational units (CUs) to derive topography-based subgrid units (TGUs). This study evaluates the capability of the TGUs to capture surface heterogeneity within grid- versus watershed-based CUs. For this purpose, TGUs are derived for the grid- and watershed-based CUs at four equivalent spatial scales (1o, 0.5o, 0.25o, and 0.125o for grid-based and HUC07, HUC08, HUC09, and HUC10 for watershed-based CUs) over the CONUS domain. Statistical metrics are computed at CU and TGU levels at each spatial scale for comparison. Results show that compared to the grid-based TGUs, the watershed-based TGUs are superior in capturing spatial heterogeneity associated with topographic slope, land cover, and surface climate (precipitation, temperature, and snow water equivalent (SWE)), despite their similar capability in capturing topographic elevation. This improved capability of the watershed-based TGUs is consistently found across all spatial scales examined. At the finest spatial scales (0.125 and HUC10), the watershed-based TGUs better capture the observed precipitation, temperature, and SWE than the grid-based TGUs at 94%, 84%, and 72% of the SNOTEL sites, respectively, highlighting the potential advantage of the watershed-based TGUs for improving accuracy and realism in ESM simulations. The data used to evaluate the capability to capture land surface heterogeneity by the topography-based subgrid structures of grid-based and watershed-based computational units include (1) input datasets that represent variability of land surface heterogeneity caused by topography [Lehner et al., 2008], land cover [Didan, K., 2021], and climate [Thornton et al., 2022]; (2) outputs of statistical metrics calculated to evaluate the capabilities of the topography-based subgrid structures of grid-based and watershed-based representations; and, (3) point climate data obtained from the SNOTEL sites utilized to evaluate capability to capture observed variability of climate fields. The data files are organized as follows: Input data: Topography: DEM (dem.zip) Slope (slope.zip) Raster watershed IDs (watershed_raster_IDs.zip) Watershed boundaries (watershed_boundaries.zip) Climate: Gridded data: Precipitation data: Gridded monthly precipitation data for the year 2015 (prcp.zip). Temperature data: Gridded monthly maximum temperature data for the year 2015 (tmax.zip). Snow water equivalent data: Gridded monthly snow water equivalent data for the year 2015 (swe.zip). Point data Point observation data: precipitation, temperature and snow water equivalent measured at the SNOTEL sites (SNOTEL_data.zip). Site information data: Information about the SNOTEL sites (SNOTEL_siteInfo.zip). NDVI: High resolution (250 meter) NDVI data used as a proxy for the land cover spatial patterns (NDVI.zip). Output data: Statistical metrics (e.g., standard deviation and range) for the grid-based representation (grid_based_statistical_metrics.zip) including: Surface elevation Topographic slope NDVI Climate variables Statistical metrics (e.g., standard deviation and range) for the watershed-based representation (watershed_based_statistical_metrics.zip) including: Surface elevation Topographic slope NDVI Climate variables Tools: Code (scripts.zip): Python scripts used to calculate the statistical metrics to evalute the capability of the grid-based and watershed-based TGUs to capture land surface heterogeneity.
keywords: Land surface heterogeneity, Earth System Models, small-scale variability, subgrid heterogeneity, topography, watershed-based representation

Maria_FloodQFMax.tif (m^3 s^(-1)). Maximum fluid flow discharge through a particular pixel (flow width is equal to cellsize = 10 meter). Maximum wood flow discharge through a particular pixel (flow width is equal to cellsize = 10 meter). Value is taken at moment of maximum total flux (fluids + solids). Erika_Deposits.tif (m). Deposit depth of solid-fluid mixture, in meters, at the end of the simulation. Erika_FloodHFMax.tif (m). Depth of slope failure in meters. This value is the depth of the failure plane relative to the surface elevation (DEM). A depth value of 0 indicates no slope failures took place. Erika_FloodHSMax.tif (m). Maximum flow height of fluids, in meters relative to surface elevation. Erika_FloodQFMax.tif (m). Maximum flow height of solids, in meters relative to surface elevation. Note: this value does not have to occur simultaneously with the maximum fluid flow height, although it generally does. Erika_FloodQSMax.tif (m^3 s^(-1)) Maximum fluid flow discharge through a particular pixel (flow width is equal to cellsize = 10 meter). Value is taken at moment of maximum total flux (fluids + solids). Data format GeoTIF Source data Global data sets, except for the DEM (LiDARDEM) and historical rainfall. This data was produced as part of the ForestCO2 project (EO and in situ based information framework to support generating Carbon Credits in forestry), which was funded by the Science Fund of the Republic of Serbia, grant no. 6686. The Canopy Height Map (CHM) for Serbia was produced using the model from https://www.nature.com/articles/s41559-023-02206-6, applied to the 5 images with the least cloud cover from the period May-September for each year in the 2020-2024 period. Final predictions for each of the 5 years were obtained by averaging the predictions from the individual models for all images of that year. The output was then masked to exclude pixels with CH<5m and to exclude pixels with no vegetation (for this, the SCL maps from the Sentinel-2 L2A products were used). Forest Above Ground Biomass (AGB) is modelled by adapting the power equation from the paper https://essd.copernicus.org/articles/15/4927/2023 where the authors estimated yearly AGB for France using the tree canopy height. We have slightly adapted the coefficient from the paper to produce the Serbia AGB map, with the final equation for relating the height and biomass of a single tree being Biomass = 0.6 x H^1.9. Forest disturbance is derived from the 2020 and 2024 CHM layers by subtracting the latter from the former to produce the total canopy height change for the time period. The change layer is filtered to exclude the pixels with change smaller than 10m, to exclude the changes caused by agricultural activities and the Canopy Height model (in)accuracy.

This dataset provides high-resolution Leaf Area Index (LAI) reference maps for validating global LAI products. It includes a total of 258 high-resolution reference LAI rasters which are available across 105 locations in 25 countries, with spatial resolutions depending on the sensor (e.g., 30m for Landsat, 10m for SPOT). The maps contain LAI effective values and are organized by validation study, country, and location, with standardized filenames for easy processing. The dataset is available for public access on Zenodo and can be used for further analysis and validation of LAI products. description: This repository contains the data used to generate the figures for the submitted manuscript "BIOPERIANT12: a mesoscale resolving coupled physics-biogeochemical model for the Southern Ocean". Contents Model input: INPUTS: ocean model input/grid files PISCES_INPUTS: BGC input files OBC: open boundary forcing WEIGHTS: weight files for ERA interim forcing Manuscript files: data: files used to generate manuscript images config, src, notebooks: Python code and Jupyter notebooks used to generate images figures, supplementary: manuscript figures and supplementary figures Abstract: "We present BIOPERIANT12, a regional model configuration of the Southern Ocean (SO) at a mesoscale-resolving 1/12 degree. This is a stable, ocean–ice–biogeochemical configuration derived from the Nucleus for European Modelling of the Ocean (NEMO) modelling platform. It is specifically designed to investigate questions related to the mean state, seasonal cycle variability and mesoscale processes in the mixed layer and within the upper ocean (<1000 m). In particular, the focus is on understanding processes behind carbon and heat exchange, systematic errors in biogeochemistry and assumptions underlying the parameters chosen to represent these SO processes. The dynamics of the ocean model play a large role in driving ocean biogeochemistry and we show that over the chosen period of analysis 2000–2009 that the simulated dynamics in the upper ocean provide a stable mean state, as compared to observation-based datasets (themselves subject to biases such as sparsity of data, cloud cover, etc.), and through which the characteristics of variability can be described. Using ocean biomes to delineate the major regions of the SO, the model demonstrates a useful representation of ocean biogeochemistry and partial pressure of carbon dioxide (pCO2). In addition to a reasonable model mean state performance, through model–data metrics BIOPERIANT12 highlights several pathways for improving Southern Ocean model simulations such as the representation of temporal variability and the overestimation of biological biomass."

This dataset offers a compilation of variables pertinent to the first 8 days of the 2016 Fort McMurray (Horse River) wildfire. It comprises hourly data over an 8-day period (May 1–8, 2016) for 11,750 grid cells, each measuring 250\,m × 250\,m. The spatial grid consists of 125 cells along the east–west (x-axis) direction and 94 cells along the north–south (y-axis) direction, centered around Fort McMurray, Alberta, Canada. This dataset has not been fully validated yet.

description: The European Wetland Map (EWM) improves the current state of knowledge on wetlands across Europe by locating, assessing and merging the latest geospatial data, e.g., on the distribution and types of floodplains and wetlands – coastal, mineral and peatlands in a bottom-up approach. It brings together existing data into a comprehensive, easily accessible resource to make wide spread European wetlands visible and enhance their analysis, understanding and management. The approach is described in the attached report. The EWM is made up of individual datasets for each of the countries included. A polygon and a raster dataset on the geographical distribution of the wetlands considered is available on country basis in an ArcGIS geodatabase and as a country-specific Geo-TIFF collection (grid size: 1 arcsecond). This work is part of the research and innovation projects “ALFAwetlands- Wetland restoration for the future” Grant Agreement No. 101056844 and “WET HORIZONS” Grant Agreement No. 101056848, funded by the Horizon Europe Framework Program of the European Union. Moreover, this work is part of the project "Building the European Peatland Initiative: a strong alliance for peatland climate protection in Europe", Grant Agreement No. 81290291. This project is part of the European Climate Initiative (EUKI) of the German Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Climate Action (BMWK). Data description Monthly global merged passive ocean color satellite retrievals (spanning September 1997 to December 2024) of the following variables (at 0.25 degree spatial resolution): mesozooplankton numerical abundance, biomass, and diel vertical migration; particle size distribution power-law slope (not used in the derivation of the mesozooplankton data, included here for completeness), particle size distribution scaling factor N0 (differential numerical concentration at reference diameter of 2 micrometers) - original and tuned versions. The tuned version is used in the derivation of mesozooplankton data. Associated estimates of partial uncertainty are also included, as well as relevant ancillary data such as the tuning coefficients for N0, and latitude/longitude grids. For details on the PSD data retrieval algorithm and N0 tuning, see Kostadinov et al. (2023; https://doi.org/10.5194/os-19-703-2023) and associated manuscrupt assets (data set and scientific code linked therein). Extensive metadata is included in the netCDF files. Also included is browse imagery - these maps are produced using the original resolution 4 km data. The maps use the 'cividis' colormap (Nuñez et al., 2018; https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0199239; https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0199239.s002). The MATLAB(R) code adapted here for 'cividis' is due to Ed Hawkins (http://www.met.reading.ac.uk/%7Eed/viridis.m). The data set is based on input monthly ocean color remote-sensing reflectance (Rrs) from the ESA/PML OC-CCI v6.0 data set (Sathyendranath et al., 2019; https://doi.org/10.3390/s19194285). The data set citation specific to v6.0 is Sathyendranath et al. (2023), https://doi.org/10.5285/5011d22aae5a4671b0cbc7d05c56c4f0 Modeling, analysis and data production (including climatologies and uncertainties) were performed using the original 4 km resolution data set in sinusoidal projection. The data set provided here (including the original uncertainty imagery) has been re-projected to equidistant cylindrical projection (unprojected lat/lon) and downsampled to 0.25 degree spatial resolution. Important Notes: The mesozooplankton variables are computed using a global constant value of the PSD power-law slope of 4.0. The variable retrieved PSD slopes are included for completeness. The extrapolation of the PSD is discussed, for example, in Jennings et al. (2008; https://doi.org/10.1098/rspb.2008.0192). See also Sheldon et al. (1972; https://doi.org/10.4319/lo.1972.17.3.0327), Hatton et al. (2021; https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.abh3732) and Tekwa et al. (2023; https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.028302). Note that the retrievals of mesozooplankton variables presented here are based on theoretical ecosystem size structure assumptions and the PSD retrieval based on phytoplankton modeling (Kostadinov et al., 2023; https://doi.org/10.5194/os-19-703-2023). A time lag can thus be expected between abundances of phytoplankton to which the PSD retrieval is assumed to be sensitive here, and the resulting mesozooplankton variables. Preliminary investigations indicate that certain locations can have time lag as measured against the Behrenfeld et al. (2019; https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-019-1796-9) satellite CALIOP lidar DVM data (e.g. 2 months at BATS), but no consistent time lag was found globally. No time lag has been applied here at the monthly scale. In addition, preliminary validation results against the in-situ BATS zooplankton data (https://simonscmap.com/catalog/datasets/BATS_Zooplankton_Biomass and Steinberg and Cope (2025; https://doi.org/10.26008/1912/bco-dmo.881861.5)) are quite satisfactory, but further global validation/comparison with these and additional data sets (MAREDAT mesozooplankton (O'Brien and Moriarty (2013; https://doi.org/10.5194/essd-5-45-2013)), satellite CALIOP lidar DVM (Behrenfeld et al. (2019; https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-019-1796-9)) is ongoing/pending. Scientific Code Scientific code in MATLAB(R) is also included. Function/script and variable names are mostly self-explanatory. The operational code to generate the mesozooplankton data needs only MATLBA(R) and no additional toolboxes. Also included is code for the optimization used to compute the empirical correction(tuning) for the N0 parameter, as well as code to compute climatologies. This additional code also needs the following MATLAB(R) toolboxes: Statistics and Machine Learning Toolbox (R), Optimization Toolbox (R), and Global Optimization Toolbox (R). Code to generate the PSD products themselves is provided elsewhere (Kostadinov et al., 2022): https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.6354653 Corresponding author Dr. Tihomir S. Kostadinov (tkostadinov@csusm.edu) Acknowledgements Funding: NASA grant #80NSSC22K0284 and NASA grant #80NSSC19K0297. Support from California State University San Marcos is also acknowledged. Mike Behrenfeld and his team (Robert O'Malley in particular) are acknowledged for useful discussions and sharing lidar DVM data and offering support with the data. Camila Serra-Pompei and Nils Haentjens are acknowledged for the very useful discussions. We also acknowledge ESA, PML and the OC-CCI team for creating the OC-CCI v6.0 data set, and we thank all data providers and algorithm developers/providers, individuals and institutions contributing to the input satellite data sets (NASA, NOAA, ESA and/or EUMETSAT) and the creation of the OC-CCI v6.0 merged satellite data set. DigitalGlobe(R) and predecessor companies GeoEye, Inc.(R) and ORBIMAGE(R) are also acknowledged for their role in SeaWiFS data acquisition. We acknowledge the BATS zooplankton and MAREDAT zooplankton in-situ data set providers, contributors and authors, as well as the satellite CALIOP lidar DVM data providers, contributors and authors. Links to relevant manuscripts/data sets are provided above. Modeling, analysis, data processing and computations, as well as visualization and file production were performed in MATLAB(R). Erik Fields, ESA, BEAM (Brockmann Consult GmbH) and NASA are acknowledged for the re-projection algorithm. We thank Alois Schlögl for ideas how to deal with NaN values and downsampling using 2D convolution. Hexa.Terra is an AI-ready agroclimatic assistant and scientific model, designed to harmonize agricultural decisions with the geometry of natural cycles [8]. Quick Access to the Assistant For direct interaction with Terra AI – Smart Farming : → chatgpt.com/g/g-6811dc59beb88191b10e56533d2e1bcc-hexa-terra-lunar-agro-ai-for-drought-yield HexaTerra is an applied iteration derived from ∆ngular Theory, a unified framework modeling space-time as a discrete angular structure. By translating lunar rhythms (Δθ₀) [15], soil moisture (T(s)) [1] and effective water entropy (S_eff(s)) [9] into angular variables, it becomes possible to: • predict yields, • anticipate water stress [7], • synchronize sowing with lunar phases [15]. ▸ Scope and interest of the model This model does not rely on any empirical adjustment: it transforms plant growth into a mathematically quantified resonance between soil, climate and lunar cycles [4]. It is aimed at farmers, cooperatives, and agricultural collectives (GAEC), both in developed and emerging regions, who wish to leverage natural dynamics as a strategic lever for agronomic decision-making, regardless of technological or financial constraints. → The economic gain displayed is deliberately conservative. → The agronomic and ecological gain, not monetized here, is based on indirect but documented effects: ⤷ Increased resilience to droughts [7][19] ⤷ Reduction in treatments thanks to more uniform emergence [8] ⤷ Better regularity of sowing over several seasons [15] ⤷ Transition from a reactive logic to a preventive strategy based on predictable cycles ❇️❇️❇️ Table of Contents 1. ∆ngular – Module Terra (France) 2. ∆ngular HT Key Variables 3. Adapted Agricultural Equation 4. Concrete Applications 5. Optimization of Seeding 6. Recommended Database 7. Operational Protocol 8. Simulation Python 9. Validation Terrain 10. Fictitious case – Soft wheat farm (Brittany) 11. Conclusion 12. Scientific Framework and Institutional Limitations 13. Citations ❇️❇️❇️ 1.∆ngular – Module Terra (France) The Hexa.Terra module applies the geometric structure of ∆ngular theory to contemporary agricultural issues. It links three fundamental dimensions: → Natural cycles (moon, seasons, plant growth) [8] [15] → Soil moisture (retention, root dynamics, sensors) [3] [6] [11] → Water stress (evapotranspiration, irrigation, resilience) [7] [10] [14] The whole thing is expressed through a mathematical framework based on the discrete angular quantification ∆θ₀ [9], allowing: • represent biological rhythms in the form of stable waves [15] • integrate climatic and pedological data into a predictive model [2] [4] [5] • anticipate water disruptions and optimize agronomic decisions [1] [14] What Hexa.Terra Offers →Forecasting Tool (3–10 Days Ahead) The strength of the model lies in its ability to predict when the critical threshold τ̃ > 0.6 will be crossed — before visible water stress occurs. It does this by factoring in: - Lunar dynamics (∆θ₀), which influence root absorption - Available water capacity (T(s)) - Soil complexity (S_eff) - Growth rate (s) You can anticipate stress before it's even detectable by a tensiometer. →Integrated View: Soil + Climate + Growth + Lunar Rhythm It’s not just a “dry alert.” The model evaluates: - Can the plant absorb what’s left in the soil? - Does the lunar phase enhance or inhibit root activity? - Is the crop at a vegetative stage that increases vulnerability? This allows you to fine-tune irrigation doses, or postpone interventions if the soil buffering capacity is high (high S_eff). →Automated, Math-Based Alerts Using a Raspberry Pi or a simple Python script, you can: - Connect your local ETP data - Integrate NDVI input (from Sentinel-2 or ground sensors) - Trigger automated alerts every day This lightens your daily monitoring burden, especially across multiple fields. Conclusion If your irrigation is already well managed, Hexa.Terra won’t replace your expertise. But it can: - Help you anticipate critical events up to 5 days in advance - Highlight high-risk zones - Standardize and scale your monitoring if you want to automate part of the workflow. 2. ∆ngular Terra Key Variables The module is based on a translation of natural cycles and pedoclimatic conditions into angular variables. These quantities are standardized to adapt to any type of crop and terroir. → Δθ₀: Lunar/phenological cycle [8], [15] [radians ∈ 0 to 2π over 28 days] → Encodes the position in the lunar cycle, used to synchronize sowing and anticipate peaks in growth or water vulnerability. → T(s): Soil water retention capacity [3], [6], [11] [value ∈ 0 to 1] → Ratio between the water actually available and the capacity in the field. Data from humidity sensors or SoilGrids/Sentinel databases. → S_eff(s): Effective water entropy [4], [9], [12] [mm/mm] → Represents the complexity of the soil by combining its texture, organic matter (OM) and vegetation index (NDVI). The higher S_eff, the more the soil can regulate water variations. → τ̃: Water stress index [7], [10], [14], [19] [value ∈ 0 (optimal) to 1 (crisis)] → Defined by the square root of the evapotranspiration deficit: τ̃ = √(1 – ETR/ETP). Critical threshold set at 0.6 in most scenarios. → s: Standardized phenological stage [2], [20] [value ∈ 0 (germination) to 1 (maturity)] → Encodes the progress of the crop. Can be estimated automatically via NDVI, phenocam monitoring or entered manually. Why does the Hexa.Terra model anticipate stress earlier than classic sensors? →τ̃ index based on the ETR / ETP ratio τ̃ = √(1 − ETR / ETP) It can respond within hours to a drop in root absorption, while a tensiometer only reacts after available water decreases. →Coupling with the Moon (∆θ₀) The model knows that certain lunar phases modulate root activity. For example, around days 10 to 18 of the lunar cycle (waxing moon), plants absorb more water. → So water tension during this phase is more serious than during the waning moon. →Soil buffering capacity (S_eff) The model takes into account your soil texture and organic matter. It can say: “OK, the soil looks fine, but the moon is pushing stronger absorption → warning: imminent risk.” Examples of early alerts : Situation: T(s) = 0.7, very high ETP, and strong NDVI Tensiometer says: “All good.” Hexa.Terra says: “τ̃ = 0.62 → red alert” Situation: Moon = day 12 (∆θ₀ ≈ 2π/3), NDVI rising Tensiometer says: “No drought yet.” Hexa.Terra says: “Root absorption at maximum → imminent stress” Hexa.Terra detects water stress potential earlier than field sensors. → It allows you to act 1 to 3 days sooner, and sometimes reduce your water use. 3. Adapted Agricultural Equation Potential_Yield(s) = κ × (Δθ₀)² × exp(−τ̃² / (4 × S_eff(s))) × [1 + ε × cos(Δθ₀ × δ × s × T(s))]^β Parameters: • κ: basic yield (5 t/ha wheat, 7 t/ha corn) [4] • ε: seasonal amplitude according to the climatic zone (0.2 to 0.6) [13] • δ: root factor according to depth (1.0 to 1.5) [12] • β: adaptation coefficient (1.2 to 1.5 for extensive crops) [17] Dynamic variables: → Δθ₀: lunar phase in radians (0 to 2π over 28 days) [8] → τ̃: water stress index, defined by √(1 − ETR/ETP) [10], [14] → S_eff(s): effective water entropy (MO, texture, NDVI) [3], [9] → s: plant growth stage (0 = germination, 1 = maturity) [2] → T(s): water retention capacity, measured or estimated [3], [11] Use : This equation is designed for ∆ngular.Terra simulators in Python. It allows you to: → cross yield peaks with lunar phases [15] → anticipate water shortages and adjust irrigation [14], [19] → modulate fertilization according to the evolution of S_eff(s) [12] 4. Concrete Applications The prediction of water stress is based on a central indicator: τ̃, normalized water stress index. Formula used: τ̃ = √(1 − ETR / ETP) where: ETR = actual evapotranspiration ETP = potential evapotranspiration [10] This expression allows a direct estimation of water tension in the soil from climatic and biological data [7], [14]. Critical threshold: → τ̃ > 0.6 for more than 10 days ⇒ automatic irrigation alert [14] This alert can trigger: • a volume recommendation (in mm) • an adjustment according to soil texture and growth stage [4], [12] Compatible data sources: • IoT sensors such as capacitive tensiometers (30 cm) [11] • Local weather stations or cooperative networks [13] • Satellite data (NDVI + surface temperature) [3], [20] Update: The τ̃ index is dynamically updated in the Terra module, via field measurements or open APIs (FAO, Sentinel, NDVI). It provides an operational bridge between ∆ngular variables and real irrigation needs [6], [18]. 5. Optimization of Seeding In the ∆ngular.Terra module, the sowing date is synchronized with the angular dynamics of the lunar cycle, coded by the variable Δθ₀. Formula: Δθ₀ = (2π × Lunar_day) / 28 [8], [15] This angular quantification makes it possible to identify windows where pedoclimatic and gravitational conditions converge. Recommended window for sowing (waxing moon): • Δθ₀ ∈ [π/3, 2π/3] • Corresponds to days 9 to 18 of the lunar cycle • Period of ascending flows favorable to root growth Empirical correlations observed: • ↑ emergence speed • ↑ post-sowing water stability • ↑ resistance to early stresses (beating, drought) [7] Effective fertility – ∆ngular formula: S_eff(s) = 0.3 × clay + 0.5 × MO + 0.2 × NDVI [4], [12], [16] → Weighting validated by INRAE (n = 2000 profiles, France) Field use: • NDVI measured by Apogee or Sentinel-2 sensor [20] • Clay content from SoilGrids or local analyses [3] • MO estimated in % dry weight via laboratory or agronomic base [4] This information is injected directly into the ∆ngular equation to adjust the sowing strategy to soil dynamics. 6. Recommended Database The ∆ngular.Terra module works by integrating public, reliable, and updatable data. Each variable is based on a validated source that is compatible with a field interface. T(s) – Soil moisture [3], [11] • Source: SoilGrids (ISRIC), Sentinel-1 (ESA) • Resolution: 100 m (raster) • Update: weekly to daily • In addition: capacitive probes (e.g.: Watermark) Δθ₀ – Moon Phases [8], [15] • Source: Ephemeride API (ephemeride.io) • Accuracy: ±0.5% (orbital calculation) • Conversion: Δθ₀ = (2π × J) / 28 • Compatible with smartphones, Raspberry Pi, Excel τ̃ – Water stress index [1], [10] • Source: FAO AquaCrop or direct calculation • Update: hourly (if weather sensor) • Formula: τ̃ = √(1 − ETR / ETP) • Compatible sensors: Davis, Decagon s – Phenological stage [2], [17] • Source: PhenoCam, Phénoclim, AI monitoring • Format: [0, 1] (germination → maturity) • Frequency: daily (AI or visual) • Option: manual annotation if no AI 7. Operational Protocol The ∆ngular.Terra module is based on a two-phase protocol: automated collection of field data, then minimal calibration. Data collection [5], [3], [8] • API integration: - WeatherStack (temperature, humidity, ETP) [5] - SoilGrids (texture, humidity) [3] - Ephemeride.io (lunar phases) [8] • Frequency: every 6 to 24 hours • Support: Raspberry Pi, local PC, Python or Excel Model calibration [4], [12], [15] • Key parameters: - β: elasticity factor (1.2–1.5) ⇨ high if extensive cultivation / unstable climate - ε: climate amplitude (0.3–0.5) ⇨ higher in semi-arid conditions • Method: - Manual calibration over 3 to 5 campaigns - AI option: if NDVI history available [12], [20] 8.Simulation Python Jupyter Workflow + Real-Time Dashboard [1], [6], [11], [20] → This Python code transforms agricultural data (lunar phases, soil moisture, vegetative growth) into dynamic yield forecasts. It generates automatic alerts when the critical water stress threshold (τ̃ > 0.6) is exceeded. Field sensor compatibility: • Capacitive tensiometers (humidity at 30 cm) [11] • Local weather stations (temperature, rain, ETP) [5] • Free NDVI (Sentinel-2 or Apogee sensors) [20] Technical integration: • Python script connected to a Raspberry Pi or MQTT module [6] • Update frequency: 6 to 12 hours • Interface: Jupyter Notebook or embedded web dashboard import numpy as np from typing import Union class DeltaNgularTerra: """ Simplified agricultural interface for the ∆ngular.Terra model """ def __init__(self, culture_type: str = "wheat"): """ Initialize with default parameters depending on the culture type """ self.presets = { "blé": {"kappa": 5.0, "epsilon": 0.3, "delta": 1.0, "beta": 1.2}, "corn": {"kappa": 7.0, "epsilon": 0.4, "delta": 1.1, "beta": 1.3}, "riz": {"kappa": 4.5, "epsilon": 0.5, "delta": 1.2, "beta": 1.4} } self.params = self.presets.get(culture_type.lower(), self.presets["blé"]) def predict_yield( self, lunar_day: Union[int, float], # Day of the lunar cycle (1-28) soil_moisture: float, # Relative soil moisture (0-1) soil_quality: float, # Composite soil quality (0-1) growth_stage: float, # Growth stage (0=germination, 1=maturity) evapotranspiration: float # Actual ET/potential ET ratio (0-1) ) -> float: """ Predicts yield in tonnes/hectare with input verification """ # Validation of inputs inputs = [lunar_day, soil_moisture, soil_quality, growth_stage, evapotranspiration] if any(not 0 <= x <= (28 if i ==0 else 1) for i, x in enumerate(inputs)): raise ValueError("Values out of range (see docstring)") # Converting agricultural parameters -> ∆ngular variables delta_theta = (2 * np.pi * lunar_day) / 28 # Lunar day -> radian conversion T = soil_moisture S_eff = soil_quality s = growth_stage tau_tilde = np.sqrt(1 - evapotranspiration) # Water stress # Calculation of yield term_angular = (delta_theta**2) * (1 + self.params["epsilon"] * np.cos(delta_theta * self.params["delta"] * s * T))**self.params["beta"] term_stress = np.exp(-tau_tilde**2 / (4 * S_eff)) return self.params["kappa"] * term_angular * term_stress def generate_irrigation_alert( self, current_yield: float, predicted_yield: float ) -> str: """ Generates a simple irrigation alert based on yield deviation """ threshold = 0.15 # 15% deviation deviation = (predicted_yield - current_yield)/current_yield if deviation < -threshold: return "🔴 Drought alert: Irrigation recommended" elif abs(deviation) <= threshold: return "🟢 Optimal Levels" else: return "🟠 Sur-irrigation possible" # Simplified usage example if __name__ == "__main__": # Initialization for a wheat crop model = DeltaNgularTerra("wheat") # Input data "in agricultural language" predictions = model.predict_yield( lunar_day=14, # Full moon soil_moisture=0.65, # 65% moisture soil_quality=0.72, # Composite quality growth_stage=0.4, # Tallage evapotranspiration=0.55 # 55% of ETP ) alerte = model.generate_irrigation_alert(current_yield=4.5, predicted_yield=predictions) print(f""" ∆ngular.Terra Agricultural Report ============================== -
